new_statements.quote: Most Lojban words are stressed on the next-to-the-last, or penultimate, syllable. In counting syllables, however, syllables whose vowel is y or which contain a syllabic consonant (l, m, n, or r) are never counted. [...] Similarly, syllables created solely by adding a buffer vowel, such as [ɪ], are not counted. [...] Primary stress is required on the penultimate syllable of Lojban content words (called brivla). Lojbanized names may be stressed on any syllable, but if a syllable other than the penultimate is stressed, the syllable (or at least its vowel) must be capitalized in writing. Lojban structural words (called cmavo) may be stressed on any syllable or none at all.
new_statements.citation: Cowan, John Woldemar. 2016. The Complete Lojban Language, version 1.1. Fairfax, VA: The Logical Language Group.
new_statements.locator: Chapter 3, Section 3.9 'Syllabication And Stress', p. 43 (PDF p. 43); corroborated ch. 4 sec. 4.3 p. 52 (brivla property 3) and sec. 4.2 p. 52 (cmavo).
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: copies we hold (584 pp., text layer, title page 'The Complete Lojban Language / John Woldemar Cowan / A Logical Language Group Publication / Version 1.1, Generated 2016-08-26') opened with extracted text. Section 3.9 'Syllabication And Stress' runs pp. 42-44; on printed p. 43 (= PDF p. 43) the quoted passage appears word for word: 'Most Lojban words are stressed on the next-to-the-last, or penultimate, syllable. In counting syllables, however, syllables whose vowel is y or which contain a syllabic consonant (l, m, n, or r) are never counted. (The Lojban term for penultimate stress is da'amoi terbasna.) Similarly, syllables created solely by adding a buffer vowel, such as [ɪ], are not counte…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the penultimate syllable, where syllables whose nucleus is schwa (y), a syllabic consonant, or an epenthetic buffer vowel are skipped in the count. This is obligatory (and word-boundary-defining) for content words (brivla); names (cmene) default to penult but may bear lexically marked stress elsewhere (written with capitals); function words (cmavo) have no required stress (convention: first vowel of disyllabic cmavo), except that a stressed syllable immediately before a brivla must be followed by a pause.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Three levels (primary, secondary, weak). Secondary stress is 'optional and non-distinctive', used for emphasis/contrast, follows speakers' native habits, and must never create a false primary stress inside a brivla. Weak (no) stress is required on syllables with y, a syllabic consonant, or a buffer vowel.
new_statements.exceptions: Syllables with y, syllabic l/m/n/r, or buffer vowels are invisible to the count and can never be stressed; cmene may carry non-penultimate stress if marked by capitalization (e.g.ARMstrong.); cmavo are free (any syllable or none); primary stress may not fall on a syllable directly preceding a brivla unless a pause intervenes.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, prescriptive (designed language): stress is part of the word-resolution (parsing) algorithm, so penultimate stress on brivla is definitional. Statement covers citation and connected-speech forms alike; phrase-level emphasis is relegated to optional secondary stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Lojban (jbo, lojb1234), the LLG-defined logical language (offshoot of Loglan, logl1234 is a distinct Glottolog entry). CLL is the language's official defining reference grammar, so the stress rule is prescriptive/definitional rather than a field description; no dialect issue.

new_statements.quote: Lojban words of more than one syllable are stressed on the next-to-last, or penultimate, syllable. (The apostrophe counts as a syllable break: blari'o is stressed as blaRI'o.) Syllables for which the vowel is y are not counted in determining penultimate stress, nor are syllables counted in which the letters l, m, n, or r occur in their syllabic forms, with no other vowel in the same syllable. (Thus, lobypli = LO,by,pli, .uacintn. = .UA,cin,tn., kat,rin. = KAT,r,in.) In Lojbanized names, a speaker may retain a semblance of native pronunciation of the name by stressing a non-penultimate syllable. In this case, capitalization is used to mark the abnormal stress, as in DJOsefin.
new_statements.citation: Nicholas, Nick & John Cowan (eds.). 2003. What Is Lojban? /.i la lojban. mo (Level 0 book). Fairfax, VA: The Logical Language Group.
new_statements.locator: Ch. 2 'Overview of Lojban Grammar', printed p. 20 (PDF p. 28); corroborated p. 17 (PDF p. 25), p. 21 (PDF p. 29, cmene), p. 22 (PDF p. 30, brivla), p. 24 (PDF p. 32, cmavo), and ch. 4 'Linguistic Issues', p. 74 (PDF p. 82)

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and the same counting conventions (y and syllabic consonants skipped, apostrophe = syllable break) as the existing CLL statement (Cowan 2016, ch. 3 sec. 3.9); the Level 0 text is essentially a condensed version of the CLL rule, and adds the explicit note that cmavo are exempt.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of every polysyllabic word, counting only syllables whose nucleus is a full vowel: syllables with the buffer vowel y and syllables with a syllabic l, m, n or r are skipped in the count. Names (cmene) may keep their source-language stress, marked in writing by capitals; brivla (content words) are always penultimately stressed; cmavo (particles) need not be, and a run of cmavo written as one word is stressed as separate words (p. 24: 'you don't have to stress pareci as paREci'). Ch. 4 p. 74 restates this as 'the morphological default of penultimate stress' and says there are no tones or pitch phonemes.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; p. 74 (ch. 4) mentions only that words are spoken 'in a speech stream with a rhythmic stress pattern' (p. 74 / PDF p. 82) with no rule given.
new_statements.exceptions: Names (cmene) may bear non-penultimate stress to imitate the source language, marked by capitalization (DJOsefin.iuNAItet,steits. /.iunaitet,STEITS., pp. 17, 20-21). Cmavo 'need not be penultimately stressed, though they often are if they have more than one syllable' (p. 24). y-syllables and syllabic-consonant syllables are invisible to the count (p. 20).
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe standard Lojban (the CLL 'Standard Lojban' of the Logical Language Group). Lojban is a constructed language with no dialects at issue; the only variation discussed is in Lojbanized foreign names, which may keep source-language stress (English vs American vs Turkish for Istanbul, English vs French for Robert/Juliette).

new_statements.quote: Capital letters are not normally used in Lojban. We use them in non-Lojban words (like Pierre) when the stress of a word is different from the Lojban norm. The norm is to put the stress on the last-but-one syllable; so, for example, kurmikce 'nurse' is kurMIKce, not KURmikce. The name Juliette would be written DJUli,et. if pronounced in an English way, but juLIET. if pronounced as in French. [p. 2] ... The final point is stress. As we've seen, Lojban words are stressed on the penultimate syllable, and if a name has different stress, we use capital letters. [p. 5]
new_statements.citation: Turner, Robin & Nick Nicholas. c. 2001. Lojban For Beginners (velcli befi la lojban. bei loi co'a cilre). The Logical Language Group (online textbook).

new_statements.relation_note: Same penultimate placement as the existing CLL statement and as work 0; less detail (no counting conventions).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress on the last-but-one syllable is the norm for Lojban words; Lojbanized foreign names may carry the stress of the source language, in which case the stressed syllable is written in capitals (DJUli,et. vs juLIET., roBER.istanBUL., maDRID., san.salvaDOR.).
new_statements.exceptions: Only names (cmene) are said to deviate, with capitalization marking the non-penultimate syllable (pp. 2, 5, 9). Unlike CLL and the Level 0 book, this beginners' textbook does not mention that y-syllables or syllabic consonants are skipped in the count, nor the cmavo exemption. The PDF is the 2002 published edition ('Published 2002'; preface dates lessons 9 and 12-15 to 2001), the same work as the c. 2001 online textbook.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe standard Lojban (the CLL 'Standard Lojban' of the Logical Language Group). Lojban is a constructed language with no dialects at issue; the only variation discussed is in Lojbanized foreign names, which may keep source-language stress (English vs American vs Turkish for Istanbul, English vs French for Robert/Juliette).
